text:
Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural director/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.

It shouldn’t have to happen that way, though. It’s a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. You’re already lost in the sauce once you start identifying with the way you see them, like she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me. I don’t mean this as a clinical diagnosis, but I use it almost diagnostically in my own life. If a woman says, “You’re such a great guy. Of course you have flaws like anyone, but I love you,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “You’re perfect. I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the BPD splitting happens, private hatred can replace worship, and then come public accusations, rewriting the whole past and treating every flaw as proof that the person was fake all along. Sometimes the woman who thought I was perfect later accuses me of thinking I’m perfect.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

For example, I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine.
reader: Someone being adored early in a relationship, deciding whether that is love or a warning sign.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
